newsitem.title: SPAIN: Electric protocol readies Spain for competition.
newsitem.headline: Electric protocol readies Spain for competition.

text.p: A sweeping plan to liberalise the Spanish power sector signed between the government and five top electricity firms aims to ready the industry for competition.

The new protocol, signed late Wednesday, phases out financial buffers over 10 years and gives electricity firms until 2007 to wean themselves off government support. They will still be compensated for certain costs during that period.
The deal allows electricity firms to continue to impose an extra charge on electricity tariffs to compensate 1.9 trillion pesetas ($14.62 billion) of fixed costs.

The fixed costs, known as "sunk" or "inefficiency" costs, refer to those costs clocked up by the government in areas such as investment in redundant nuclear assets and subsidies for national coal usage.
The protocol has divided up just over 75 percent of these costs among companies, while the remaining 25 percent will be determined by work groups to be set up to study the issue.

The protocol also lays down guidelines to open the sector to competition in electricity generation, approving the introduction of new competitors as well as the liberalisation of fuel supplies, except Spanish coal.
It was also agreed that electricity tariffs would fall every year until 2007.

On the sunk costs issue, Industry Minister Josep Pique said the 1.9 trillion pesetas included 300 billion as incentives for national coal. A further 200 billion pesetas will correspond to compensation for extraordinary investments.
Total costs recognised to adapt to competition will be 1.5 trillion, he added.

With reference to the division of costs among the electricity companies the protocol has allocated 568.7 billion pesetas to Endesa, 431.5 billion pesetas to Iberdrola while Union Fenosa will take 204.8 pesetas.
Sevillana will account for 85.5 billion pesetas and Fecsa's share will be 159.1 billion.
The transition period takes effect from the start of 1998.
But one electricity company refused to sign the protocol on the grounds that the decision on how the remaining 24.6 percent was to be returned to the companies was unfair.
Hidroelectrica del Cantabrico said the aspects of the protocol were too vague and could cause damage to the company's assets in future.
Moreover, the firm's main shareholder Catalan savings bank La Caixa put its considerable weight behind Cantabrico's move.
But Pique told a press conference that Cantabrico would forfeit its compensation because of this posture but would still have to shoulder a share of the costs.
"Because they didn't sign the protocol, Hidrocantabrico's part is zero," Pique said.
Shares in Cantabrico were sharply lower on Friday after the news, shedding 70 pesetas to 4,420 by 1500 GMT.
